decisions.quote: We begin by reproducing AJR’s results in simple regressions showing that both ex-colonies that were more urbanized in 1500 and ex-colonies that had higher population densities in 1500 had lower incomes in 1995. We use AJR’s data for all variables, including the estimated urban share of population in 1500, which is from Bairoch (1988) and Eggimann (1999), estimated population density in 1500 based on McEvedy and Jones (1978), and 1995 real GDP per capita, originally from the World Bank.
decisions.reason: The paper re-analyses the original study's (Acemoglu, Johnson, and Robinson 2002) dataset and sample of former colonies, first reproducing the exact base regressions in Table 1 columns (1) and (4) and then testing alternative variable constructions (ancestry-adjusted 1500 development indicators and alternative proxies), controls, sample restrictions, and terminal years. Under the codebook, re-analysing the original study's own data is a reproduction rather than a replication.

decisions.quote: We are able to reproduce the AJR reversal in terms of the territorial entities that constitute present-day countries. But we show that with respect to the people who live in countries and their descendants, there was no reversal. AJR (2002) demonstrated their reversal on the basis of two main indicators of development in 1500: the rate of urbanization, and population density. We find that in the large fraction of AJR’s once-colonized countries sample for which we can estimate year 1500 ancestry, the descendants of people from societies that were more urbanized and more densely populated in 1500 have higher, not lower, incomes today.
decisions.location: Introduction, p. 1, lines 51-59 (see also Section I.A, p. 5, lines 179-181 and Footnote 11, p. 14, lines 547-549)
decisions.reason: Because the study is a reproduction, outcome is coded on the two reproduction axes. On outcome_computation, the authors obtain exact replications of AJR's base-sample regressions in columns (1) and (4) of Table 1 ('computationally reproducible'). On outcome_robustness, the original reversal-of-fortune finding is not robust: adjusting AJR's 1500 indicators for population ancestry reverses the sign of the relationship to persistence of fortune, replacing the 1500 proxies yields statistically insignificant territorial estimates in the base sample, and dropping the six neo-Europes and city-states renders AJR's territorial urbanization coefficient statistically insignificant ('robustness challenges').
